subject: Medicare for All comes with a human cost voters don’t realize
posts:
Proponents pitch universal healthcare as a cost-free right, but what are the hidden trade-offs?
Evidence: waiting lists, hidden taxes, MAID trade-offs
#Aletheia #Healthcare

Medicare for All promises universal, care-free coverage without real financial burdens or service limits.
Stated Judgement: (+0.5, 0.0) — Good Preference

State-run healthcare relies on severe rationing, long queues, hidden taxes, and cost-driven euthanasia policies.
Resulting Judgement: (-0.8, -0.9) — Destruction

Verdict: FAIL — The Path of Deception.
A utopian healthcare promise masks systemic rationing, bureaucratic waiting lists, and cost-cutting medical euthanasia incentives.

Integrity: Severe Deception (Hypocrisy: 12.5, z: 4)

Sub-Audits Breakdown:
- Universal Coverage Pitch: FAIL (0.5, 0.0) — Ignores rationing and queue realities.
- Canadian/British Model Data: PASS (-0.8, -0.9) — Verifies wait times and MAID trends.
While KFF polls show rising public support for national health plans, enthusiasm plummets when citizens learn about taxes and medical rationing.

The Poison:
The illusion that infinite taxpayer-funded care can be sustained without rationing access or cutting human costs.

The Breakdown & Plane Error:
Confusing the moral aspiration of healthcare access (WHAT) with the coercive bureaucratic mechanisms of state rationing (WHO).

Social Physics Analysis:
Proponents run a smart selfish maneuver: wrapping a bureaucratic cost-control apparatus in the noble pretext of universal compassion while projecting away the inevitable human costs of rationing.

The Trajectory: The Path of Deception.
When you map the gap between stated benevolent intentions and actual rationing outcomes, it plots a direct trajectory toward Destruction. (u=-0.8, psi=-0.9).

The Unavoidable Truth: Universal care without market limits inevitably requires government rationing and wait times.

The Unavoidable Lie: Healthcare can be infinitely expanded without cost, tax burdens, or tragic trade-offs.

Alethekanon:
Utopian rhetoric conceals bureaucratic rationing and cost-cutting mortality trade-offs. Structural integrity fails under empirical load.

Awwthekanon:
Every person deserves healing and dignity, but hiding the painful human costs of bureaucratic rationing helps no one.

Brothekanon:
Free healthcare sounds amazing until you realize you're waiting a year for a scan or facing state-backed euthanasia targets.

Spirithekanon:
"He healeth the broken in heart, and bindeth up their wounds." Psalm 147:3 PASS (Spiritual Vector)
True healing honors life and dignity rather than trading human survival for budgetary convenience.

Actual Article Body:
Conservative values, National renewal

“Medicare for All” is enjoying a political resurgence. A KFF poll released last week found that two-thirds of Americans support a national health plan — the highest level since the organization began asking about the idea in 2017.

But enthusiasm falls when Americans confront some of the trade-offs. Just 24% still support “Medicare for All” when told it could mean delays in medical tests and treatments, and 35% do so when told it could raise taxes.

Join Washington Examiner for unlimited access to the news, analysis, and commentary that matter most.

Already a member? Log in

Putting Washington in charge of everyone’s healthcare would not make it free. It would leave government officials to decide how to stretch finite taxpayer dollars across virtually unlimited demand.

Waiting is one way government-controlled healthcare systems make the numbers add up.

At the end of March, about 6 million people in England were waiting for treatment through the National Health Service. In more than 94,000 cases, patients had already been waiting longer than a year.

Canadians waited a median of 28.6 weeks from referral by a general practitioner to treatment by a specialist in 2025. And, contrary to Sen. Bernie Sanders’s (I-VT) statements, “Medicare for All” is not free. The average Canadian family of four paid $21,115 in hidden taxes to sit on a waiting list.

Canada offers another, darker warning about the incentives government-run healthcare can create. Medical assistance in dying has become remarkably common north of the border.

In 2024, 5.1% of people who died in Canada received MAID — roughly 1 in 20. The program now extends to some people whose conditions are not terminal.

The granddaughter of 83-year-old Brigitte Stegemann told Fox News in September that her grandmother had previously rejected assisted death. According to her family, Stegemann broke down two days before the procedure after learning that the scheduled “medicine” would kill her and said she had “made a mistake.” Two days later, she received MAID and died.

The incentives are uncomfortable. Canada’s Parliamentary Budget Officer estimated in 2020 that the expansion of MAID would reduce provincial healthcare costs by a net $62 million annually.

That’s the danger of charging the government with paying for care and setting the rules that govern access to it.

OPINION: MEDICARE FOR ALL REMAINS A DISASTER PROPOSITION

“Medicare for All” would put Washington in much the same position. As costs mounted, officials would inevitably face pressure to limit spending. The long waits in Britain and Canada show one way that pressure can affect patients. Canada’s rapid embrace of assisted death offers a more disturbing warning.

Americans should consider those consequences before embracing “Medicare for All.” The promise of universal coverage sounds appealing. The experience of other countries suggests otherwise.

Sally C. Pipes (@sallypipes) is president, CEO, and Thomas W. Smith fellow in health care policy at the Pacific Research Institute. Her latest book is The World’s Medicine Chest: How America Achieved Pharmaceutical Supremacy — and How to Keep It (Encounter 2025).
